articles.title: The Memo: Bond market turmoil heightens midterm risks for Trump and GOP
articles.summary: Turbulence in the bond markets, fueled primarily by rising anxiety about government debt, is creating one more headwind for President Trump and the GOP as they move toward challenging midterm elections. Bond yields ticked up again on Tuesday, with the yield on the U.S. Treasury 10-year note hitting its highest point since January 2025. The…
articles.body:
Turbulence in the bond markets, fueled primarily by rising anxiety about government debt, is creating one more headwind for President Trump and the GOP as they move toward challenging midterm elections.

Bond yields ticked up again on Tuesday, with the yield on the U.S. Treasury 10-year note hitting its highest point since January 2025.

The yield on the 10-year as recently as late February, just before the start of the war with Iran, was around 4 percent. Now, it sits at about 4.8 percent.

An increase on this scale, which sounds modest, can have major repercussions on the government’s expenses to manage its massive debt load, which recently hit $40 trillion.

Rising bond yields also swiftly seep into consumer lending, nudging up interest rates on mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt.

That’s bad news for Trump and his party, given that numerous polls show the cost of living to be at the top of voters’ lists of concerns. Trump repeatedly gets lower poll ratings on that issue than on any other.

The complex moves of the bond markets rarely make headlines. When they do, it’s often bad news.

On Tuesday, the Drudge Report blared “Bond Yields Soar, Global Panic, Stock Crash Imminent?” across the top of its home page.

Even if that seems a tad overexcitable to most experts, there’s no denying the growing nervousness gnawing at the markets.

In basic terms, the bond markets are getting edgy about several factors, which are combining into a powerful storm.

Prime among those is the U.S.’s rising debt load and the lack of evidence that there is political will in either party to do much about it.

There’s also sticky inflation, and the possibility that the Federal Reserve will have to raise interest rates. There’s the related issue of the war, which increases volatility especially with respect to energy prices, sustaining inflationary pressure.

Internationally, other nations are also grappling with rising debt and deficits. Finally, the AI boom is being fueled in significant measure by companies issuing their own bonds, thus competing with the U.S. federal government for creditors’ business.

Trump has, characteristically, insisted that all will be well. Speaking with reporters Monday, he returned to a familiar refrain — that interest rates should be lower.

“When we do well, they shouldn’t have to raise interest rates. They should, in many cases, lower [rates],” he said . “When we’re doing well, we become a better credit. When you become a better credit, you’re supposed to cut rates.”

It’s far from clear that even Kevin Warsh, Trump’s recently confirmed chair of the Federal Reserve, agrees.

Last week, Warsh said the Fed could have “work to do” to bring inflation down to its target of 2 percent from its current rate of 3.4 percent. The comment was widely seen as an acknowledgment that rates might have to rise.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has tried to shore up confidence — with mixed success.

In media interviews on Monday and Tuesday, Bessent has talked up the robustness of the market for U.S. bonds.

“If there were a problem in the bond market … then people would be selling U.S. bonds and buying other countries’ bonds. But we are the best-performing market,” he told CNBC’s Sara Eisen on Monday.

Still, Bessent’s move last week to double federal buybacks of long-term debt offered only a very brief balm to the bond markets. Yields briefly fell before resuming their climb.

Jessica Riedl, a budget and tax fellow at the Brookings Institution, told this column that such a move can actually backfire because “it tells financial markets that Treasury is concerned about long-term interest rates but too feckless to do anything about it.”

Riedl also argued that the larger issue of rising yields could hurt Republicans come November’s elections.

“The polls have not looked good for Republicans because voters are clearly worried about the economy — in particular when President Trump had promised such dramatic economic gains. He said prices would begin falling on Day 1.”

Conservatives see the electoral implications differently, even as they acknowledge that U.S. government debt is a long-term problem.

“I don’t think folks follow the bond market. What they follow are their home economics — what things cost them,” Mick Mulvaney, who served as the director of the Office of Management and Budget during Trump’s first term, told this column.

Still, in terms of the rising concerns evident in the bond market, Mulvaney said: “Fiscal conservatives like me have been wondering for two decades when this was going to happen.”

He stressed that he did not see the situation right now as a crisis but “it’s a small trend-line.”

Some economic experts sound a broadly similar tone.

Allison Schrager, a senior fellow at the Manhattan Institute, said that on one hand, “debt crises tend to happen very slowly and very quickly — and it’s a reason why I’ve been very concerned about debt for a long time.”

But Schrager also suggested that, by historic standards, the current mix of inflation and bond yields was not that remarkable.

“Really, yields are not that high relative to what they normally are,” she said. “Inflation is about 3 percent. Yield on the 20-year is around 5 percent. That’s not crazy. Historically, that’s pretty consistent.”

Still, Democrats are betting voters are more likely to be casting ballots in November with a general sense of economic malaise rather than with an in-depth knowledge of historic bond yields.

“They are already taking it on the chin because of Iran, the cost of living, the cost of healthcare and all that,” Democratic strategist Mark Longabaugh said.

“You add on higher interest rates, and it’s all going to be laid at the feet of Republicans,” he added, “And I think it’s going to get worse over the next nine weeks.”

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: A third Trump impeachment looks inevitable, but what kind?
articles.summary: As the final primaries wrap up and we head into the full gale of the general election campaign season, the consensus is that Republicans are all but certain to lose their very narrow House majority. If you ask Nate Silver and his team, they’ll say there’s an 86 percent chance of Democratic control with the…
articles.body:
As the final primaries wrap up and we head into the full gale of the general election campaign season, the consensus is that Republicans are all but certain to lose their very narrow House majority.

If you ask Nate Silver and his team, they’ll say there’s an 86 percent chance of Democratic control with the highest probability of a 15-seat majority for the blue team. The gang at Decision Desk HQ sees a slightly closer contest, forecasting a 66 percent probability that Democrats take over , with the fat part of their bell curve right around a 12-seat Democratic majority. But nobody seems to think that what amounts to a two-seat current majority for House Republicans will survive whatever is brewing up for this fall.

That’s a real bummer for Republicans, given that the GOP spent all that money and effort on their mid-decade gerrymandering blitz only to see it become their Maginot Line. If you look at the current ratings from the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter or Sabato’s Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia, you see that the GOP is only netting out three or four sure gerrymandered pickups — nowhere near enough to save them.

Certainly that’s how Washington is behaving. The closed-door meeting between Jared Kushner — President Trump’s son-in-law and ambassador without portfolio — and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) certainly suggests an air of Democratic inevitability. So does the capitulation from House Republicans on punting the rest of their legislative agenda until after the election.

How big a prospective Democratic House majority may be certainly matters, most of all to Jeffries. He’s going to be getting at least a half dozen more members of the “squad” or the Justice Democrats, or whatever you like to call the blue version of the Tea Party. They will be intent on making it as hard as possible for the would-be Speaker to get anything done. But if Democrats have a great year instead of just a good one, the extra seats will come from Republican-leaning swing districts likely to produce pragmatic new representatives.

But whether Jeffries is under siege from the start or has a 12-seat cushion to protect him from extortionate demands, there’s one thing that won’t be avoided: a third impeachment of Donald Trump.

There are already a few Democrats saying that it would be a pointless distraction to launch yet another failed impeachment and that the party should use a new House majority to focus on issues that matter to the American people. This sounds good and would make a certain amount of sense, but for the fact that a new House majority wouldn’t be doing much of anything at all.

Let’s take the high end of the register for Democrats this fall and suppose that they have a substantial cushion in the House and manage to flip the Senate. Even in that world, Democrats would be nursing a one- or two-seat Senate majority that would surely include red-state moderates unwilling to go along with radical moves.

And as far as legislating goes, the presidential veto power makes the Senate a lot easier to blockade than the Strait of Hormuz. No, the only work that’s likely to be done in a divided Washington is going to be around shutting down the government and then trying to reopen it. Get your furlough counters ready, folks.

The typical answer for the party with Congress in periods of divided government is oversight. That’s certainly how Republicans busied themselves in the last two years of the Biden administration, when Hunter Biden got more airtime than pharmaceutical ads. But Democrats won’t even have that option, at least through normal means. In his first term, Trump already made clear that neither he nor the members of his administration will comply with hostile congressional subpoenas. They will not come, nor will they produce the documents demanded.

Democrats could then hold theatrical hearings to “call attention” to the refusals, but those pass over the public consciousness like clouds on a spring zephyr. Congress can hold members of the administration in contempt, but as both parties have proven, it’s a toothless threat. Congress lacks police powers, and the Trump Justice Department isn’t going to help. There’s also the power of the purse, but Democrats will already be in continuing resolution hell from the start. Lawmakers can always sue, but the courts — even before the current one — have taken an expansive view of executive privilege.

Courts, though, have always had a different standard when it comes to the matter of impeachments, when Congress gets its greatest degree of judicial deference. In the three modern impeachments, the very act of beginning the process has unlocked congressional superpowers. And Trump would be daring them to do it — he of the crypto billions, the gifted jumbo jet, the drug boat kill teams and the budget impoundment. The biggest challenge would be deciding what to include and what to leave out.

Of course, if Republicans hold the Senate in November, those powers will quickly wear off. Trump’s first two impeachment trials were perfunctory matters conducted in a Republican-controlled Senate, lasting 20 days in 2020 and just five days in 2021. This is the world in which a fast, failed impeachment may actually help Trump rally his party around him.

A Democratic Senate, however, would be different. In 1868, a hostile Senate spent 82 days on the impeachment trial of President Andrew Johnson. The 2027 version could make that look like a cakewalk, with week after week of testimony and document dumps. And the rules say that all the while no other actions may come to the floor. It’s the ultimate gridlock.

Those may be the real stakes in the battle for the Senate. Not whether Trump is impeached again, but whether it is another stunt or something that actually draws blood.

articles.title: El-Sayed walks political tightrope in Michigan with Hasan Piker
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed is walking a political tightrope in the Michigan Senate race as the Democratic nominee enters the final stretch of his campaign, looking to shore up support among skeptical Jewish voters without outright disavowing controversial left-wing streamer Hasan Piker. El-Sayed has also faced pressure to disavow Piker, who campaigned for El-Sayed during the primary…
articles.body:
Abdul El-Sayed is walking a political tightrope in the Michigan Senate race as the Democratic nominee enters the final stretch of his campaign, looking to shore up support among skeptical Jewish voters without outright disavowing controversial left-wing streamer Hasan Piker.

El-Sayed has also faced pressure to disavow Piker, who campaigned for El-Sayed during the primary and has come under fire for several controversial statements, including suggesting Jewish Americans who support Israel have themselves to blame for violence that may befall them.

El-Sayed condemned the comments but has resisted calls to disavow Piker.

On Monday, he made clear he had no intention of denouncing Piker, pushing back in an interview against what he described as a “massive effort to cancel Hasan” and suggesting Piker’s critics were taking the streamer’s remarks out of context.

“They’re trying to equate him and David Duke, and him and Nick Fuentes,” El-Sayed said on “ The Breakfast Club” radio show. “The fact that they’re working so hard to character assassinate him suggests that there is a disjunct there between what he’s actually saying and what people hear him saying who actually pay attention.”

“If anybody starts to pick you apart out of context, it’s never done in good faith,” he added.

The approach has left some Jewish Michiganders unconvinced, questioning whether an apology El-Sayed offered over the weekend — for saying “hurt people hurt people” in reaction to the March attack on the Wolverine State’s largest synagogue — was sincere.

Joan Lowenstein, the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus’s endorsement chair, said she was glad to hear El-Sayed call the March incident a “terrorist attack,” but she described his apology as a “carefully crafted statement” that addressed the timing of his remarks, not the substance.

The attacker on the Michigan synagogue was Lebanese and had family — including a brother who was a high-ranking Hezbollah commander — who died in an Israeli airstrike a week before the attack in Michigan.

“He apologized for putting it in context only a couple of days after the attack happened, and so that kind of left open the question: Why would you have to put a terrorist attack on preschoolers in any kind of context?” Lowenstein said.

The apology was just one step El-Sayed has taken to try to win over Democrats who may have opposed him during a divisive primary. El-Sayed’s campaign also confirmed that it is hiring a Jewish liaison as the candidate works to build bridges in the community.

But it’s unclear if that will be enough for El-Sayed to really make inroads with his critics, particularly as his association with Piker lives on.

Michigan-based political consultant Adrian Hemond said both the apology and the addition of a position dedicated to Jewish outreach are steps in the right direction.

“They definitely have their work cut out for them, in terms of getting folks back in the boat who have concerns about some of the views that he’s expressed. And it’s probably pretty late in the game to get started. Absentee ballots go in the mail in two-and-a-half weeks in our fair state,” Hemond said. “But, you know, it’s a start.”

Matt Grossmann, a political science professor and director of the Institute for Public Policy and Social Research (IPPSR) at Michigan State University, said El-Sayed’s apology “doesn’t seem to have stopped the concerns, but it’s taken as evidence that he’s listening to them.”

He also noted the debate has largely played out among political elites, rather than voters.

“The other side of it is that he doesn’t want to come off as a flip-flopper or someone who’s abandoning his positions, or to sound too much like a politician,” Grossmann added. “So I think that’s the other consideration that’s driving his decisionmaking.”

El-Sayed has blasted efforts to “cancel” Piker or to dismiss him as just a “single streamer from California” who does not speak for his campaign. Part of that may be by necessity.

“He invited the guy to come to Michigan to campaign for him in a primary election,” Hemond said. “You can’t un-ring that bell.”

“You can say he doesn’t want to talk about a streamer from California,” he continued. “Bro, you brought the streamer from California here to campaign for you. It doesn’t matter if you want to talk about it. People are going to talk about it.”

Politically, El-Sayed’s approach to Piker could find some support in new polling from the IPPSR . The poll, released Tuesday, shows some voters — as expected — are inclined to back Democratic gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson, Michigan’s secretary of state, but are not yet on board with El-Sayed.

But the poll also shows a big age divide — with some young voters supporting only El-Sayed’s campaign but not Benson’s.

“That does suggest that there is a potential downside” to splitting with Piker, Grossmann said. “So I think he’s trying to toe that line.”

Grossmann said El-Sayed could benefit from preserving his image of authenticity and being different from other politicians who quickly cave to party demands.

“There is a general potential positive narrative for El-Sayed that he’s not a normal politician and that he’s willing to take on the establishment, including people in his own party that he doesn’t want to lose,” Grossmann said. “And so I think that’s part of the consideration for how much he’s willing to step out, say, against Piker.”

articles.title: Trump seeks affordability wins down midterm homestretch
articles.summary: President Trump is taking every available avenue in his effort to appeal to voters on affordability as frustrations over high prices and economic uncertainty show no signs of subsiding nine weeks out from the midterms. Trump met with oil and gas retailers and refineries at the White House as oil prices jumped again amid the…
articles.body:
President Trump is taking every available avenue in his effort to appeal to voters on affordability as frustrations over high prices and economic uncertainty show no signs of subsiding nine weeks out from the midterms.

Trump met with oil and gas retailers and refineries at the White House as oil prices jumped again amid the latest strikes in the U.S. war in Iran. The meeting came after Trump announced an oil deal with Venezuela last week, which he also said would lower energy prices.

The president has amplified his efforts to lower drug prices this week, announcing new Medicaid pricing agreements with nine midsize biotechnology and pharmaceutical companies on Monday.

And in a recognition of consumer frustration at the grocery store, Trump has pressed ahead with a temporary pause on beef import tariffs despite fierce backlash from cattle ranchers and their GOP allies in Congress.

The efforts come as numerous polls show Trump’s approval rating declining , which could impact Republicans running up and down the ballot in November.

Seventy-one percent of Americans, including 40 percent of Republicans, said they disapprove of how Trump is handling the cost of living, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll released Monday.

“Once you’ve reached Labor Day, the narrative is pretty well set in, but does that mean there’s not anything else you can do? You’ve seen him address beef prices and reduce tariffs,” said Marc Short, who served as Trump’s legislative director in his first term and as chief of staff to former Vice President Mike Pence.

Democrats have argued that Trump rolling back tariffs in an effort to lower costs for consumers is a clear admission that tariffs were increasing prices for Americans in the first place, which Trump and his officials have consistently denied.

“They know that that’s an option for them, but they’re just reluctant to do it because they’re committed to the policy,” Short said of tariffs.

Another national Republican operative was hopeful the party could still persuade voters in the final stretch.

“Ads are really just going up on air,” the operative told The Hill on condition of anonymity. “The real spending starts now, post Labor Day, and we’re going to see a ton of resources pour into these districts, and a lot is going to change over the next couple of weeks.”

“I think we already have the ammunition needed in terms of what our members need on the campaign trail and what we need for ads,” the operative said. “What the president is doing, I think, is a great boost and a good supplement.”

Trump is sitting on an enormous war chest with his MAGA Inc. super PAC, which could help amplify efforts like TrumpRx, a platform he touts as creating historic reductions in some drug prices.

Under Monday’s agreement, another nine drug companies were added to his “most favored nation” plan, meaning they will charge state Medicaid programs the same prices for certain outpatient drugs as they charge foreign countries. Companies, in turn, will receive protection from pharmaceutical tariffs.

“I think everything is important. I would say healthcare is, to me, very important. You’re talking about life,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office following the announcement on Monday, when asked if he believes healthcare or the price of gas is more important for Americans.

The Trump administration has also sought to tackle rising energy prices through an oil deal with Venezuela. Under the agreement, the U.S. would work with a Venezuelan oil company to pump large amounts of oil from the country’s reserves.

Critics have questioned how long it will take to extract the oil from the ground, citing the cost, potential legal challenges and the state of Venezuela’s infrastructure.

Trump said Friday the agreement will “substantially lower Gas Prices for all Americans, long into the future.”

“Ultimately, prices are going to come down. Now, will it happen before the election? I can’t tell you that,” Trump told reporters.

There are outside factors that are influencing prices as well, including the resumption of U.S. strikes against Iran on Monday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average plummeted more than 400 points while U.S. oil prices hit roughly $90 per barrel and Brent crude hit roughly $95 per barrel Tuesday.

“No one wants to see prices continue to rise, so that does give us a little bit of heartburn,” said the national Republican operative.

Critics have also pointed to Washington’s trade war with Canada, which has threatened to have a particularly sharp effect on a number of states with competitive elections that happen to border Canada, including Alaska, Michigan, Ohio, Maine and New Hampshire.

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods are set to go into effect on Sept. 8.

The trade war comes after Trump spent much of the beginning of his second administration slapping tariffs on countries around the world, including U.S. allies.

“Despite the fact that Iran is a threat, was a threat, [and] needed to be dealt with, I think voters have soured on it, in part because they’ve spent at this point a year and a half being told that everything he’s doing with trade and international affairs is for the ‘national security’ interest, when it’s clearly the case that none of that is,” said Richard Stern, vice president of the Plymouth Institute for Free Enterprise at Pence’s think tank Advancing American Freedom.

“I don’t blame the American public for saying, ‘Yeah, well, is Iran a bigger threat than upholstered furniture or Canadian beef exports?’” he said.

In a statement to The Hill on Tuesday, the White House blamed the affordability crisis on Democrats and the Biden administration.

“The Democrats created the affordability crisis by unleashing the highest inflation in four decades,” White House spokesperson Olivia Wales said in a statement.

“President Trump has spent every day in office working to undo their mess and lower costs for working families by signing the largest middle-class tax cuts in history, lowering the cost of prescription drugs, permanently expanding the child tax credit, fueling wage growth, and reshoring American manufacturing to create more high paying jobs,” she added.

Inflation was higher at points during the Biden administration than where it is now, but it has gone up since Trump took office. The annual U.S. inflation rate currently sits at 3.4 percent, while it peaked at 9.1 percent in June 2022. In former President Biden’s final year in office, it was around 3.0 percent.

“People have short-term memories,” said Allen Mendenhall, a senior adviser for the Free Enterprise Initiative at the conservative Heritage Foundation. “It has been worse, and not all that long ago.”

articles.title: Lame-duck agenda balloons as Congress punts priorities until after election
articles.summary: GOP lawmakers are punting major fights — including government funding, money for the war with Iran and the extension of expanded surveillance authorities — until after the November election, setting up a bloated lame-duck agenda that will be difficult to get done by Christmas. The House on Tuesday overwhelmingly passed a bill to fund the…
articles.body:
GOP lawmakers are punting major fights — including government funding, money for the war with Iran and the extension of expanded surveillance authorities — until after the November election, setting up a bloated lame-duck agenda that will be difficult to get done by Christmas.

The House on Tuesday overwhelmingly passed a bill to fund the government until Dec. 11, initiating a major partisan fight over spending levels for defense and nondefense programs after Thanksgiving.

A senior Senate GOP aide said “a lot” is getting pushed into the lame-duck session.

“The question is whether we can put together ‘ash and trash’ on an approps bill, which I assume will be an omnibus,” the aide said, using congressional slang for a bill that collects miscellaneous provisions to be attached to a must-pass bill.

The source said Democrats might be willing to cut deals after the election if they don’t reap the windfall of seats in the House and Senate that some Democratic lawmakers are optimistically expecting.

The Trump administration has requested a historic $1.5 trillion in defense spending, which Senate Democrats have rejected as a nonstarter. Democrats have blocked spending bills from advancing in the Senate because they claim Republicans have asked for a 4.5-1 increase in defense spending compared to nondefense spending.

Then there’s a brewing fight over the Trump administration’s emergency funding request for the Pentagon, farmers struggling with drought and low commodity prices as well as long-stalled disaster relief funding.

Congress needs to act on the expanded surveillance authorities under the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) that expired in June and the $1.15 trillion annual defense authorization bill, which Democrats blocked on the Senate floor in July.

It also needs to move the farm bill, which failed to get out of the Senate Agriculture Committee in August because Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) couldn’t attend the markup, leaving Republicans without a majority on the panel.

Lawmakers will need to scramble to finish work on a bill regulating the recruitment and compensation of college athletes for use of name, image and likeness if the measure manages to pass the Senate this month. It remains to be seen if the Protect College Sports Act can get 60 votes to advance.

Adding more chaos, Republicans are still talking about passing a budget reconciliation package in the lame-duck session to fund the war in Iran and provide up to $10 billion to states to incentivize tightening regulations for voting.

All of that will get packed into the six or seven weeks of legislative session expected after the election, starting on the week of Nov. 9 and running up until Christmas, with a week of recess planned for Thanksgiving, which is on Nov. 26.

“You’ll look at an omnibus at some point, but before that I think you’re going to have a real serious discussion about bringing the Democrats in with regard to the full story why we need supplemental on defense and some other areas,” said Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.), a member of the Senate Appropriations Committee and the Armed Services Committee.

Rounds said Republicans would likely move an omnibus spending package with emergency funding for the Pentagon and other priorities, and then move a separate budget reconciliation package with funding for the six-month conflict with Iran.

But moving a budget reconciliation package will consume a lot of time on the Senate floor because it will entail first passing a budget resolution and slogging through two all-night vote-a-rama sessions.

Rounds on Tuesday acknowledged “we are” piling a lot on the lame-duck calendar and that it’s a “good question” whether the ambitious agenda can pass, especially if Democrats pick up a large number of House seats and win control of the lower chamber.

Democrats also think they have a chance of winning the Senate majority but face a tougher path. They would need to gain four seats, including at least some races in Republican-leaning states such as Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas.

“It all depends on what the election outcome is and what people’s desires are to be here and work their way through,” Rounds said. “If leadership can come with an agreement to get certain things done on a consensus basis that the White House is willing to go along, yeah, we can get some things done fairly quickly.”

The Senate is planning to vote on a motion to proceed to the Clarity Act, a bill backed by the cryptocurrency industry to establish a regulatory framework for digital assets.

The crypto measure is expected to fail because Democrats are demanding strong conflict-of-interest provisions related to the Trump family’s crypto investments.

“They have a real problem with getting seven Democrats on board,” a GOP aide said of the Clarity Act.

Rounds, a member of the Banking Committee, acknowledged “it does not look good right now” for the Clarity Act “because I don’t think there’s been an agreement on ethics yet coming out of the White House.”

The Senate will then move to a vote on the college sports bill, approved by the Senate Commerce Committee with bipartisan support. If the motion to proceed to the bill has 60 votes, senators could spend up to two weeks considering amendments before voting on final passage.

But Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is expected to punt the annual defense authorization bill and a deal to extend FISA’s lapsed surveillance authorities until after the Nov. 3 election.

“I think the NDAA will come together after the election,” Rounds said of the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA).

Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), chair of the Senate Budget Committee, has been working over the recess on a budget resolution that he hopes to bring to the Senate floor this fall to pave the way for a budget reconciliation package that could pass with a simple majority and avoid a Democratic filibuster.

But vulnerable GOP colleagues such as Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) have made it clear that they don’t want to face another vote-a-rama on the Senate floor before Election Day, which would give Democrats a chance to force them to vote on tough issues that could provide fodder for campaign ads.

That means the budget resolution and follow-up reconciliation bill will get dropped into the lame-duck bucket, but the crowded agenda has some GOP aides predicting that reconciliation 3.0 won’t happen before January.

articles.title: James Carville decries 'idiot' Hasan Piker, orders DSA to change its name
articles.summary: Democratic strategist James Carville branded Hasan Piker an "idiot" and demanded the Democratic Socialists of America drop "Democratic" from its name.
articles.body: Democratic strategist James Carville expanded his critique of left-wing streamer Hasan Piker on Tuesday, branding him an "idiot" and saying he cannot answer for Piker’s band of "left-wing idiots." Piker, a self-described socialist streamer who campaigned with Democratic Michigan U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, has emerged as a leading voice on the left as democratic socialists continue to gain influence. "There's two things that I know about Hasan Piker. One, he's an idiot, and two, he's not a Democrat. So, I don't answer for idiots, and I don't answer for people who are not Democrats," Carville said on "The Story." JAMES CARVILLE VOWS TO ABANDON DEMOCRATIC PARTY IF FAR-LEFT HASAN PIKER BECOMES LEADING VOICE Tuesday’s comments were not the first time the longtime Democratic strategist has targeted Piker. Carville recently pledged to leave the Democratic Party if Piker were to become a leading voice within the party and said an "overwhelming majority" of Democrats agree. "I understand that I'm a Democrat. I'm part of a big coalition, a big tent, and we all have an admission policy," Carville told Fox News. "But thank God Hasan Piker doesn't want in our frat, because we don't want him." JAMES CARVILLE RESPONDS TO 'VICIOUS' PROGRESSIVE DEMOCRATS TRYING TO DRIVE HIM OUT OF THE PARTY Piker, who drew criticism after saying "America deserved 9/11" during a stream in 2019, expressed a similar disdain for Carville. "We got John Fetterman, James Carville, fantasizing about leaving the party — I'm like, you're sweetening the deal," Piker said during a recent stream. Fox News Digital reached out to Piker for comment. Carville criticized the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), arguing the platform benefits by associating itself with the Democratic Party and ordered the far-left organization to redact "Democratic" from its name. CARVILLE TORCHES DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS AS 'PACK OF FOOLS,' PRAISES AOC'S POLITICAL EVOLUTION "What I would tell a Democratic socialist — ‘If you hate the Democratic brand so much, why use our words? Go call yourself something else. Call yourself the Socialists of America,’" Carville said. Carville argued that the DSA’s values and policy positions, including defunding the police, do not align with those of the Democratic Party. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Don't put the first word in your title 'Democratic' because… that's our party. That's the party of civil rights. That's the party of women's rights. That's the party of balanced budget. That is the party of prosperity," he said. "Don’t use our name. Make up your own name," he added. Carville previously warned that Democratic socialists are dragging the party’s brand "through the mud."

articles.title: Texas Dem candidate to hold high-dollar Hollywood fundraiser while GOP gathers in Dallas: 'Fake cowboy'
articles.summary: James Talarico heads to Hollywood for a second celebrity fundraiser as Ken Paxton and Trump rally Republicans in Dallas for the midterm push.
articles.body: Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico is set to travel to Los Angeles in September for a high-dollar fundraiser with Hollywood celebrities, according to a report. Politico reported that "Lost" co-creator Damon Lindelof and his wife, Heidi, will host a fundraiser for Talarico in Brentwood on Sept. 10. Tickets for the event start at $500 and go as high as $13,500, according to the outlet. This will be Talarico’s second Hollywood fundraiser in a few months. The first was held in June and was described by Page Six Hollywood as a "glitzy Dem fundraiser" at the home of Hollywood producer Peter Chernin. Fox News Digital reached out to the Lindelofs and Chernin for comment. Meanwhile, Talarico’s opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, will gather in Dallas for the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention, along with President Donald Trump and other Republicans. The same night Republicans rally in Dallas, former President Barack Obama will headline a Democratic House fundraiser in New York, according to The New York Times. The events put prominent Democrats on the coasts while Republicans gather in Texas. Fox News Digital previously reported that donors from outside Texas accounted for roughly 50% of the funds raised by Talarico, according to first-quarter campaign finance records. TALARICO SAYS THE DIVIDE IS 'TOP VS. BOTTOM' — THEN HEADS TO ONE OF AMERICA'S RICHEST DONOR ENCLAVES Talarico is taking heat from Republicans for his out-of-state fundraising. RNC spokesperson Zach Kraft told Fox News Digital that "it is no surprise that James Talarico feels more comfortable in crazy liberal California than when his handlers force him to wear a fake cowboy hat and rent a pickup truck to pretend to be a 'real' Texan." Fox News Digital reached out to Talarico’s campaign for comment but did not receive a response by the time of publication. Talarico currently serves as a progressive Democratic lawmaker in the Texas House of Representatives. Since winning the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate, Republicans have continually knocked him for his record of controversial statements, including calling God "nonbinary," saying that there are six sexes and saying that reducing meat consumption was "existential" to fight climate change. JAMES TALARICO DOESN'T DRIVE HIS OWN TRUCK IN VIRAL TEXAS CAMPAIGN AD FEATURING DODGE RAM Despite the attacks, Talarico and Paxton are running a tight race, and many Democrats believe this could be the year Texas finally flips blue. A Fox News poll from July gave Talarico a 3-point edge over Paxton, 51% to 48%, which was within the survey’s margin of sampling error. Paxton, meanwhile, has told Fox News Digital that Talarico’s lead is not surprising given his head start in the general election following his particularly messy primary runoff against incumbent Sen. John Cornyn. Speaking with Fox News on Sunday, Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said that "money is an issue" in the race. FIRST ON FOX: MAJOR CORNYN BACKER GOES ALL-IN FOR PAXTON AS GOP RALLIES AFTER RED STATE SHOCK POLL "Mr. Talarico has been raising bucketloads of money from California, Hollywood," he said. He called on Trump to help Paxton with cash, saying, "We in the Senate don’t have the money budgeted for Texas; we need help from the president." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER For his part, Trump has promised: "I’m going to help Ken Paxton, and I’m going to spend a lot of time in Texas." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Touting his history of winning the state three times on the presidential level, he said, "I’ll be going to Texas, and we’re working really hard. We want to win that race." Trump called Paxton a "very good candidate," while taking a jab at Talarico, saying, "‘Talafreako,’ they call him, because he is a little freaky."

articles.title: DeSantis endorses Florida GOP slate including Byron Donalds in governor's race
articles.summary: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis endorsed a "slate" of candidates that included GOP gubernatorial candidate Rep. Byron Donalds.
articles.body: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis endorsed a "slate" of Republicans statewide Tuesday, including GOP gubernatorial nominee U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds. "I'm endorsing the slate here tonight ... because I know it's important for the state of Florida," DeSantis said at the Florida GOP Leadership Forum in Tampa. The event showcased Donalds, Attorney General James Uthmeier, Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia and Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson. Last year, DeSantis appointed Ingoglia as CFO and Uthmeier as attorney general. Later in 2025, the governor endorsed Ingoglia for election to the CFO post. He then backed Simpson for re-election this year. TRUMP'S HANDPICKED DESANTIS SUCCESSOR WINS CROWDED GOP PRIMARY FOR FLORIDA GOVERNOR "Tonight I was honored to earn Governor @RonDeSantis’s endorsement," Donalds wrote in a post on X. "Governor DeSantis has done incredible work to make Florida the envy of America. As your next Governor, I will build on his success and defend the Florida Dream," he said. FORMER FLORIDA GOVERNOR HOPEFUL HAULED OUT OF COUNTY MEETING AFTER PROTESTING ISRAEL INVESTMENTS Donalds, who won the Florida GOP gubernatorial primary in August with the backing of President Donald Trump, will face Democratic gubernatorial candidate former U.S. Rep. David Jolly in the general election. While he is currently running for governor as a Democrat, Jolly previously served in the U.S. House of Representatives as a Republican. BYRON DONALDS SHUTS DOWN BILL MAHER'S CLAIM ON GOP PRIMARY RACISM, SAYS 'FLORIDA IS A MERITOCRACY' Under the Florida Constitution, DeSantis, who is serving his second consecutive term, is not eligible to seek another consecutive term as governor this year. articles.title: Nation’s largest teachers union under fire as controversial agenda puts century-old federal charter at risk
articles.summary: Sen. Bill Cassidy's report targets the NEA's ties to the Zinn Education Project and Rethinking Schools over curriculum glorifying political violence.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE — The head of an influential Senate committee is urging Congress to reconsider the charter of the nation’s largest teachers union, citing its far-left associations and allegedly irresponsible financial activity. In recent years, the National Education Association, which represents roughly 3 million educators, has come under fire for mobilizing students and teachers to support liberal activist campaigns, been criticized by its Jewish members for failing to address antisemitism, spent millions in membership dues supporting left-wing causes and partnered with organizations that portray political violence and far-left extremism favorably. Now, Sen. Bill Cassidy, the Republican chair of the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions, is calling on his colleagues to take a closer look at the NEA’s congressional charter. BLISTERING REPORT EXPOSES HOW NATIONAL K-12 GROUP'S DEI AGENDA IS TRICKLING DOWN TO LOCAL SCHOOLS "Children are struggling to read and to do basic math. Instead of helping students succeed, teachers’ unions are injecting a dangerous, anti-American agenda into our classrooms," Cassidy told Fox News Digital. "Parents deserve to send their children to school without worrying that they will be indoctrinated with DEI and taught that Americans have ‘misplaced faith’ in our institutions." Cassidy, in a report outlining the NEA’s activity obtained exclusively by Fox News Digital, puts a spotlight on the Zinn Education Project and Rethinking Schools — a pair of interlinked educational nonprofits that the top teachers union has collaborated with extensively. EXCLUSIVE: SPLC'S 'FAR-LEFT' 'ANTI-RACISM' CURRICULUM FOUND IN CLASSROOMS AS EARLY AS KINDERGARTEN: WATCHDOG The Zinn Education Project and Rethinking Schools, for instance, have published curricular materials that justify the actions of the Black Panther Party — a left-wing militant Black nationalist organization that operated during the Cold War — and praise its members, including those who were involved in acts of political violence, according to the report. "The Marxist and communist ideologies espoused by the Black Panther Party are inconsistent and incompatible with the foundation of the United States Constitution," Cassidy’s report, published by the HELP committee, reads. "The Black Panthers advocated for the use of armed force against police and were involved in the murders of civil servants and members of their own party." SCOPE OF SPLC'S DEEPLY EMBEDDED INFLUENCE TRAINING TEACHERS NATIONWIDE UNCOVERED IN SWEEPING REPORT Rethinking Schools also published a lesson plan where students are meant to role-play as "queer liberation" activists fighting against the "Religious Right," according to the report. Another lesson plan, titled "Expanding Intersectional Queer History in the Elementary Grades," instructs teachers on how to incorporate LGBTQ material into lessons for young students. The union has worked closely with the duo of nonprofits over the years, giving them prominent space and speaking opportunities at conferences, collaborating with them on curriculum development and nationwide teaching events, and praising and promoting their lessons. The union has also incorporated the groups’ work into educator handbooks and helped distribute their lesson plans to teachers. HOUSE GOP LAUNCHES PROBE INTO 5 MAJOR LABOR UNIONS OVER DEM SPENDING DESPITE MAGA MEMBERSHIP BASE Congress chartered the NEA in 1906 under the expectation that it would "elevate the character and advance the interests of the profession of teaching; and to promote the cause of education in the United States," a mission Cassidy and some other Republicans argue it has since strayed from. Revoking the NEA’s charter would primarily be a reputational blow to the union, as it would still be able to operate even without it. As another example of the NEA allegedly failing to live up to its charter, the HELP committee points to its involvement in the left-wing protest movements. MAY DAY PROTESTS ‘JUST THE BEGINNING’ OF STUDENT ACTIVISM PUSH, EXPERT WARNS The labor union promoted and participated in the 2026 May Day protests, which were critical of President Donald Trump and his Republican allies. In one planning webinar the NEA hosted in the lead-up to the demonstrations, educators were advised to "bring activism into the classroom," targeting children as young as three years old. Students in Chicago were reportedly encouraged by teachers to skip class for the protests, even as Chicago Public Schools see subpar reading and math competency scores. On the financial side of things, Cassidy points to data showing that, since 2015, the NEA has contributed hundreds of millions of dollars to advocacy organizations and political action committees, the vast majority of which are left-of-center. In some cases, political organizations funded by the NEA later provided members of the union’s leadership team with cushy jobs, according to the report. FAR-LEFT ACTIVIST CONFERENCE AT TEACHERS UNION HQ RAISES CLASSROOM CONCERNS "The central issue is not whether every such expenditure is impermissible. Rather, it is whether members receive sufficient transparency about how their dues are used, whether union leadership has adopted adequate safeguards against conflicts of interest and whether these expenditures advance the purposes for which members joined the union in the first place," the Senate committee report reads. Organizations funded by the NEA include the Sixteen Thirty Fund and the Tides Foundation, two of the largest Democratic-aligned dark money operations in the country, as well as millions to its own PAC, which almost exclusively supports Democratic candidates. JEWISH EDUCATORS FACE RAMPANT ANTISEMITISM IN TEACHERS UNIONS, NEW REPORT FINDS The HELP committee report also alleges that the NEA has failed to represent the interests of Jewish educators, citing an August 2025 letter where the union’s Jewish Affairs Caucus claimed its members reported "shunning, harassment and antisemitic comments" at the union’s annual assembly. While not congressionally chartered like the NEA, the American Federation of Teachers drew flak from Cassidy’s report for many of the same reasons. The report cites the AFT’s participation in "No Kings" protests against President Donald Trump, its boycott of Target over immigration enforcement and its advocacy on LGBTQ+ issues, as well as its routing of tens of millions of dollars to liberal causes, as evidence of alleged mission drift at the union. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The NEA, AFT, Rethinking Schools and the Zinn Education Project did not respond to requests for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Tuesday. The scrutiny comes as the NEA transitions to new leadership. Princess R. Moss, a former NEA vice president and secretary-treasurer, began a three-year term as president on Tuesday, succeeding Becky Pringle, who led the union for six years.

articles.title: Congress takes midterm shutdown fight off the table
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ House sends funding bill to Trump ▪ Markey coasts to victory over Moulton ▪ U.S. launches new Iran strikes ▪ Postal Service whistleblower issues warning Members of both parties came together Tuesday as the House easily approved a short-term funding measure to keep the government open into December and rule out the possibility…
articles.body:
▪ Postal Service whistleblower issues warning

Members of both parties came together Tuesday as the House easily approved a short-term funding measure to keep the government open into December and rule out the possibility of a shutdown battle with the midterms fast approaching.

The House passed the continuing resolution (CR) by a vote of 370-48, sending it to President Trump ’s desk for his signature. The Senate previously approved the legislation by a similarly wide margin last month.

The bill will keep the federal government fully funded through Dec. 11, punting any battle over spending until the lame-duck Congress ahead of the holidays.

The Hill’s Helen Huiskes notes that passing a CR so early in the year — almost a month before government funding is set to run out on Sept. 30 — is rare. But what was clear from the votes in both chambers of Congress and across both parties is that lawmakers were eager to avoid any politically risky funding battle before voters head to the polls.

This Congress has already dealt with two record-long shutdowns, as the parties battled each other over expiring health insurance subsidies and the Trump administration’s hard-line immigration policies.

Democratic strategist Doug Wilson said if either party had attempted to use the CR and the current situation to push a legislative demand, they could have faced political backlash.

“With economic headwinds from the war along with a rattled bond market, both parties had no choice but to vote on a CR,” Wilson told Morning Report.

Months ago, some Republicans predicted that Democrats would reject an agreement and shut the government down to get a political boost just as voters are casting their ballots. But Democrats have been trending upward recently and seem to like their current political standing.

Their lead in the generic congressional ballot has varied over the months but currently stands at a comfortable 6 points in the Decision Desk HQ tracker .

Trump’s approval rating has continued its downward slope as inflation and gas prices remain high amid the Iran war, which has now lasted six months despite the president’s initial expectation that it would only last four to five weeks.

Republican leadership had made clear for months that they had no interest in a shutdown fight , having suffered politically in the most recent battles. Polling mostly showed during the record-long full government shutdown last fall more people blamed the GOP for the situation than did the Democrats.

With only a few of the 12 appropriations bills passed to cover government funding for the full upcoming fiscal year, a short-term measure was the only immediate option.

“When we passed our continuing resolution over here, we knew it would change when it got to the Senate,” House Appropriations Committee Chair Tom Cole (R-Okla.) said on the floor just before the vote.

“Some of those changes I actually agree with, some of them I don’t. But they don’t really change the substance of the fact, we bought the time that we need to get through the election cycle and hopefully the time that we need to get down to serious bargaining on the other side of it.”

▪ The Hill : Lame-duck agenda balloons as Congress punts priorities.

▪ The Hill : Russia sanctions bill hits House roadblocks.

DEM DEFECTIONS : A handful of Democrats broke with their party in key votes Tuesday, but a pair of defections on a rule vote is causing particular consternation in the minority caucus.

Reps. Jared Golden (D-Maine) and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) crossed the aisle to vote in favor of advancing a group of Republican-backed bills, essentially bailing out Speaker Mike Johnson ’s (R-La.) agenda and preventing hardline conservatives from tanking the vote series.

The rule included a GOP-supported bill to denounce socialism, a key part of the party’s messaging ahead of the midterms. Eight Democrats ultimately voted with Republicans on that resolution.

The move from Golden and Gluesemkamp Perez to support the rule blindsided House Democratic leaders , who said neither member gave a heads up about their plans. The majority party traditionally votes in favor of rules, which set up debate and a final vote on a piece of legislation, while the minority party opposes them, regardless of whether a lawmaker ultimately supports a bill.

House Democratic leaders Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), Katherine Clark (D-Mass.) and Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.) put out an angry statement Tuesday night.

“The decision by two of our colleagues to blindside the entire House Democratic Caucus and join with the Republican majority to pass a procedural rule on the brink of failing represents a significant breach of trust. It is an action that necessitates a serious response, and we have asked the Committee on Caucus Rules to take this up in short order,” they said.

▪ The Hill : House censures Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) over allegations of inappropriate behavior.

The Trump administration is touting its agreement with Venezuela on what it’s describing as the “biggest oil deal in world history.” According to the White House, the U.S. will have “majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of proven oil reserves in Venezuela.” I asked State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott when that could bring relief at the pump for Americans here at home.

“We’re going to see the ability to have offtake rights over the short-term here, and then we’re going to see that scaling,” Pigott said . “We’re going to see the scaling over the next several months and years, and what’s going to happen here is the fact that we’re going to have more secure reserves, lower gas prices,” he added.

articles.title: DEI: Shiny new acronym, same old discrimination
articles.summary: Civil rights law was written to end the practice of deciding what people deserve based on the color of their skin.
articles.body:
A senior program manager at Washington University in St. Louis did exactly what every diversity, equity, and inclusion program claims it wants employees to do. She spoke up when something felt like discrimination .

In January 2025, her employer’s Office of Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion split a mandatory training into what it called “shared racial identity spaces” — in other words, Zoom breakout rooms segregated by race. She was the only Black staffer on her team, and told the office beforehand that this would leave her isolated. The university ran the session anyway.

The manager complained internally, then filed a charge with the federal Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. Her department eliminated her position months later. A university diversity official called it a miscommunication and defended the racial breakout rooms as anti-racism work.

Last month, the commission sued Washington University . Its acting General Counsel Catherine Eschbach put it bluntly: This employee was separated from her white colleagues exactly as she feared, then lost her job for objecting to it.

I have spent 30 years building governance and compliance frameworks for family offices, and I have sat as a court-designated expert witness explaining fiduciary duty to judges and juries from coast to coast. When you build a policy, you look at what it actually does, not at what its name promises.

When you sort people by race into rooms, committees, hiring pools or admissions tiers, you are discriminating by race — full stop. It doesn’t matter whose photo is on the recruiting brochure. It doesn’t matter how many anti-racist tracts or videos you force your employees to read or watch. Title VI and Title VII carry no asterisks for supposedly good intentions.

The pattern runs straight through higher education. In May, the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division found that Yale School of Medicine had studied how to use racial proxies to work around the Supreme Court’s 2023 ban on race-conscious admissions in Students for Fair Admissions . The school was admitting Black and Hispanic applicants with consistently lower grades and test scores than their white and Asian peers.

Investigators had flagged the same conduct at UCLA’s medical school days earlier. Three weeks ago, the department turned to Duke University School of Law , whose admissions statistics say it all: In 2024 and 2025, rejected white and Asian applicants had higher median LSAT scores than Black applicants who were admitted. For the 2024 admitted class, the median LSAT score for successful Black applicants was 164; for successful Hispanic applicants, it was 170; white applicants needed a 172 and Asian applicants a 173 to get in the door.

Duke had made cosmetic changes after the Supreme Court’s ruling, but then, according to the department’s findings, kept sorting applicants by race through diversity essay prompts and proxies like Pell Grant status. Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon put it plainly: Schools do not get a free pass to discriminate against white, Asian or any other students just because they believe their intentions are good.

More recently, the department added George Washington University’s medical school to the list of targeted institutions. Barred from checking race on forms, it instead used essay questions to infer race. It then inferred putatively Black students with significantly lower MCAT scores than their white and Asian peers.

In each case, the Justice Department offers the same choice: Settle voluntarily or else face a lawsuit. Columbia already agreed to a $200 million settlement that requires it to eliminate race preferences from hiring and admissions and end race-based DEI benefits. Officials say Cornell and Brown are negotiating similar deals.

Duke, Yale, and Washington University are not outliers. In May, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission sued the New York Times for denying a promotion to a white male employee under a diversity program the paper had been boasting about since 2021.

In March, Planned Parenthood of Illinois paid $500,000 to settle claims that it segregated employees by race during mandatory affinity caucus meetings and allowed white staff to be harassed under an anti-racism banner. An Asian job applicant collected another $500,000 from HCL America after a recruiter flagged him as insufficiently “diverse.”

Four major law firms signed consent agreements disavowing their own DEI hiring targets rather than face the commission in court. The White House ties this push to its 2025 order, “ Restoring Equality of Opportunity and Meritocracy, ” which says that outcome gaps alone are not proof of discrimination. This is not a handful of surprised bad actors — a business model normalized over the course of decades, now hitting the wall of federal civil rights law one case at a time.

Defenders will say that intent matters, and that DEI exists to correct generations of real discrimination, not to add to the pile. I understand the impulse. But curing an old wrong with a new sorting system built on the same premise — that a person’s race tells you something useful about how to treat him or her — just moves the wrong onto a different set of shoulders. Martin Luther King, Jr. did not march so the country could eventually pick a different favored race. He wanted the sorting to end.

Every general counsel, university provost, and human resources director should pull training slides and admissions rubrics off the shelf this week, not next quarter. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and the Justice Department now treat much of their “diversity” language as evidence of wrongdoing, not as a shield.

Boards funding programs built on racial sorting are not managing risk — they are underwriting it. Civil rights law was written to end the practice of deciding what people deserve based on the color of their skin. Giving that practice a new acronym never made it legal or moral, and it never will.

Jay Rogers is a financial professional with more than 30 years of experience in private equity, private credit, hedge funds, and wealth management.

articles.title: Madagascar ex-Senate chief Richard Ravalomanana jailed over deadly Gen Z protest crackdown
articles.summary: At least 22 people were killed and more than 100 injured during last year's unrest, according to the UN.
articles.body:
Madagascar's former Senate president has been sentenced to 10 years of hard labour over his alleged role in the violent crackdown on youth-led protests that helped bring down the previous government last year.

Richard Ravalomanana, a retired general and close ally of former President Andry Rajoelina, was found guilty of complicity in murder by a court in the capital, Antananarivo, on Tuesday.

Prosecutors accused him of giving instructions to security forces to use violence against demonstrators during the so-called Gen Z protests in September and October 2025.

Ravalomanana denied the allegations and said he would appeal against the judgement.

From prison to presidential palace: Who is Madagascar's new military ruler?

The protests began a year ago, initially sparked by anger over persistent power and water shortages, before developing into a broader movement against Rajoelina's government.

At least 22 people were killed and more than 100 injured during the unrest, according to UN figures cited by local media.

The protests eventually triggered a political crisis that led to Rajoelina's removal from power and the installation of a new administration led by Col Michael Randrianirina.

The crackdown was led by the gendarmerie, where Ravalomanana retained considerable influence at the time.

He "directed violent actions to suppress the demonstrations", a state prosecutor said in December 2025.

Ravalomanana was removed as Senate president in October, shortly after the protests, and was arrested at his home in December after failing to respond to a summons from the gendarmerie.

He was later placed in pre-trial detention at the high-security Imerintsiatosika prison outside Antananarivo, where he has spent the past seven months.

He is among several senior figures associated with Rajoelina's former government who have faced legal proceedings since the change of power. Ravalomanana is also facing a separate corruption investigation.

A former national police chief who testified at the trial backed his account, saying Ravalomanana was not part of the operational chain of command and had issued no orders to police, gendarmes or soldiers deployed during the unrest.

His lawyer questioned the evidence linking him directly to the violence.

"Is there confirmed written or verbal evidence... to accuse him?" he asked the court, arguing that prosecutors had failed to produce proof that security officers had received orders from his client.

Ravalomanana's defence team said it would challenge the verdict in a higher court.

The court dropped a separate allegation of making a death threat after ruling that the case was too old to prosecute.

Known for wearing a cowboy hat and displaying his military medals, Ravalomanana was viewed by protesters as a symbol of authoritarian power.

articles.title: The US is gobbling up Venezuelan oil, but will it lower fuel prices?
articles.summary: Analysts say Venezuelan crude is hard to extract and refine, and likely can’t replace oil stuck in the Strait of Hormuz.
articles.body:
When United States President Donald Trump announced “ the biggest oil deal in world history ” with Venezuela on August 28, he claimed it would “more than double” US oil reserves and “substantially lower gas prices for all Americans”.

Venezuela is home to the world’s largest proven oil reserves – an estimated 303 billion barrels, or about 17 percent of the global total, according to the US Energy Information Administration. But the country’s oil is heavy, sour crude and extracting and refining it is costly.

While US Gulf Coast refineries are able to process this type of oil from Venezuela, analysts have warned that, in reality, Washington’s deal with Caracas will not lower crude prices in the US in the near term.

What is in the US-Venezuela oil deal, and will it lower fuel prices in the US – or elsewhere?

What’s in the new oil deal between the US and Venezuela?

Last week, the Trump administration announced a deal that would give the US control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s proven oil reserves. That is more than one-fifth of all of Venezuela’s known oil.

To do this, a White House fact sheet has revealed, the US is creating a private joint venture with North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), which is owned by billionaire Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt , an ex-ally of Hugo Chavez, the former socialist president.

NABEP is already the second-largest operator in Venezuela after US oil giant Chevron, which is also expected to expand its oil operations in Venezuela.

The deal will give the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital a 35 percent stake in NABEP, which will “have reputable US auditors, lawyers, and advisors”, the White House said.

The White House said that “millions of barrels of new Venezuelan output will be processed through US refineries and pumped with American rigs and infrastructure, supporting billions in investment in the United States and thousands of jobs here at home”. The US will be guaranteed a right to buy 20 percent of the output at cost.

The joint venture with NABEP has capacity to produce about 200,000 barrels of crude oil per day, increasing US production as Iran’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz has spiked global oil prices, including in the US.

Venezuela’s interim President Delcy Rodriguez welcomed the oil deal, which is also expected to add much-needed funds to the state’s treasury.

The creation of the joint venture will make it easier for NABEP to operate from Venezuela, which remains under US sanctions.

The US has been importing large amounts of Venezuelan oil since President Nicolas Maduro was captured in a US military operation in January this year. Maduro was flown to the US to stand trial on guns-and-drugs charges, while his vice president, Rodriguez, was left as interim leader. She has since facilitated US access to Venezuela’s oil industry and the US has lifted personal sanctions against her.

In August, US Under Secretary of Energy Kyle Haustveit said more than 500,000 barrels per day (bpd) is now moving from Venezuela to the US – some 40 percent of the country’s national output of 1.25 million bpd.

Have US crude prices fallen since the deal was announced?

According to analysts, US crude prices have actually risen since Trump announced the latest deal.

Johannes Rauball, a senior crude oil analyst at Kpler, the global trade intelligence agency, noted that before Washington’s agreement with Caracas, US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude was trading about $83-$86 per barrel, while Brent crude – the global benchmark for oil prices – was hovering between $85-$88 per barrel.

“Since then, prices have moved even higher – with WTI pushing past $90 and Brent topping $95 per barrel – driven up primarily by heightened geopolitical risks and acute Middle East supply disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz,” he told Al Jazeera.

On Thursday morning (06:00 GMT), WTI crude futures had climbed by 61 cents, or 0.7 percent, to $90.83.

Why aren’t US crude or gas prices coming down?

According to Rauball, while the US-Venezuela deal may improve supply and, therefore, market sentiment in the longer term, near-term prices are unlikely to be impacted because of the practical difficulties of extracting oil from the ground in Venezuela.

“It will take years for this deal to result in a meaningful ramp-up in production due to Venezuela’s severe physical bottlenecks and ageing infrastructure – most notably degraded pipeline gathering systems, insufficient electrical grid support, and a lack of specialised crude upgraders,” he said.

As far as US fuel prices are concerned, he added, US refiners are already operating at maximum capacity to meet demand both domestically and abroad, leaving little room to scale up further.

“While access to heavier Venezuelan crude supplies offers the specific feedstocks US Gulf Coast refiners require, it will not translate into near-term price relief at the pump given these refining throughput constraints and ongoing operational delays,” he said.

Tracy Shuchart, senior economist at futures trading platform NinjaTrader, wrote in a post on X on August 29: “Everyone cheering the Venezuela deal thinks a flood of cheap oil is about to hit and pull gas prices down. It isn’t.

“Venezuela pumps about 1.2M bpd right now, up from just under a million. That gain came mostly from Chevron ramping up existing wells after sanctions were lifted, not from new drilling. The easy barrels are already back. The reserve number is a stock that will take decades to convert to flow,” she said.

What does this deal mean for global oil prices?

Iran’s closure of the strait, through which more than 20 percent of global oil and natural gas is shipped in peacetime, has upended global energy markets.

Shortly after the strait was closed in early March, the price of Brent crude oil rose above $100 per barrel. Before the war, it was trading at about $66 per barrel. On Thursday, Brent crude rose $1.03, or 1.1 percent, to $95.68 a barrel at 06:05 GMT.

According to Kpler’s Rauball, the immediate impact of the US-Venezuela oil deal on global crude prices remains “neutral” as current markets remain focused on short-term geopolitical supply shortages caused primarily by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

“Over the longer term, a successful ramp-up [of production] will gradually increase the overall availability of Venezuelan crude in the global market. This added volume will help increase crude supply globally over time, ultimately exerting persistent downward pressure on global oil prices further down the line,” he said.

But there are several reasons why an increased supply of Venezuelan oil ultimately cannot make up for the reduced supply of oil from Gulf producers which used to be shipped through the Strait of Hormuz.

Frederic Schneider, a nonresident senior fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, said: “The US-Israeli war on Iran took at least 10million barrels a day off the market through Hormuz. Venezuela cannot replace that, also partly because it is a different grade, namely, heavy, sour crude which competes with other heavy imports (mostly Canadian and some Mexican) rather than substituting for the lighter Gulf oil.”

Hamad Hussain, a climate and commodities economist at the United Kingdom-based firm Capital Economics, also told Al Jazeera that developing oilfields in Venezuela requires significant amounts of investment and time before more crude could be produced and sold to global markets.

“Even in the long term, the potential for political instability and high costs involved could make investors wary of committing to oilfield projects in Venezuela. This could hold back the extent to which oil supply in Venezuela increases and, in turn, limit the downward pressure on crude oil prices over the coming years,” he told Al Jazeera.

Furthermore, only a few countries have refineries capable of processing the very heavy oil which Venezuela produces. These are primarily the US, China and India.

“Refineries in Europe are geared towards refining lighter grades of crude, so there would be little interest in importing oil from Venezuela there,” Hussain said.

“The heaviness of Venezuelan crude would be a bigger problem for President Trump’s stated aim to refill the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) with crude from Venezuela. This is because storing oil from Venezuela in the SPR could cause damage to the underground caverns.

Global crude prices will, therefore, also continue to depend heavily on how the US and Israel’s war on Iran, which has paralysed the Strait of Hormuz, plays out.

So who will really benefit from this deal?

US oil companies are likely to earn the biggest gains from this deal. After the deal was announced late on Friday, shares in Chevron, currently the only big US oil company active in Venezuela, rose 2.2 percent to $206.20 on the Dow Jones index of publicly listed companies.

On Tuesday, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said several oil companies from the US and other countries are also expected to sign oil deals in Caracas this week, which will increase Venezuela’s crude oil production. These are expected to include Chevron, Italy’s Eni, India’s ONGC, Colombia’s GeoPark and the US’s GE Vernova.

Venezuelan oil production peaked above 3 million bpd in the late 1990s but plummeted after that due to lack of investment, mismanagement and US sanctions. In recent months it has been about 1.1 million to 1.2 million bpd, rising slightly since President Nicolas Maduro was abducted by US forces in January.

Wright claimed that gas prices will fall for US consumers as and when US oil companies increase their investments in Venezuela.

“The investment in these deals will massively grow available oil production, which will give downward pressure on oil prices, but the biggest kink right now in gasoline and diesel prices is refining capacity,” Wright told reporters in Venezuela, without giving any details about how refining capacity would be increased.

However, Schneider said he did not envisage many other oil companies rushing to invest in Venezuela’s oil industry. “The more fundamental problem is that the high-price shock earlier in the war has destroyed demand, which has put pressure on WTI,” he told Al Jazeera. “With a highly uncertain demand forecast and Gulf oil coming back online at some point, no company wants to put $100bn into a country as risky as Venezuela,” he added.

articles.title: Can anything stop the White House ballroom?
articles.summary: A preservationist group likely has no standing to stop the White House ballroom, the Supreme Court says. So, does anyone? Not necessarily. Let’s start with a little bit of history.
